title: Light Grating
experiment: Kapitza–Dirac effect (diffraction of matter by a standing light wave)
intro: A cloud at rest sits in the dark. Key 1 switches on a standing wave of light, a potential V sin²(πx/10) that ripples across the whole box. It exerts no net force, yet a short flash diffracts the cloud like a grating: momentum appears in steps of 2π/10. This level measures momentum. Put as much as you can into the first orders, ±0.63, and as little as possible into the undeflected order at k = 0 (the mine).
goal: Flash the light grating (key 1 on, key 1 off) to kick the cloud into the first diffraction orders, the two green discs in momentum space, then observe. The undeflected order at k = 0 is a mine.

physics.point: A thin grating multiplies ψ by a phase e^{iφ cos qx}. Expanded in plane waves, that is a ladder of momentum orders nq, with probabilities J_n(φ)², set by the pulse area φ = Vτ/2.

idea: In 1933 Kapitza and Dirac predicted that electrons should diffract from a standing wave of light, as light diffracts from a ruled grating. The roles of matter and light are swapped: here the light is the grating. It was seen with atoms in the 1980s and with electrons only in 2001.

The standing wave is a periodic potential. A short flash does not give the cloud time to move, so its only effect is a phase that varies periodically across the cloud. A periodic phase is a sum of plane waves with momenta 0, ±q, ±2q, … where q = 2π/period: the cloud splits into diffraction orders and flies apart.
How much goes into each order depends only on the pulse area: the strength times the duration. Too short a flash leaves most of the cloud at rest; too long a flash pushes it into higher orders.
maths: V sin²(qx/2) = V/2 − (V/2) cos qx. A flash of length τ (short compared with 1/recoil, the Raman–Nath regime) multiplies ψ by

maths.eq: e^{−iVτ/2} · e^{i(Vτ/2) cos qx} = e^{−iVτ/2} Σₙ iⁿ Jₙ(Vτ/2) e^{inqx}

maths: (the Jacobi–Anger expansion), so order n carries probability Jₙ(φ)² with φ = Vτ/2.
Both first orders together carry 2J₁(φ)², at most 68% at φ = 1.84, i.e. τ ≈ 1.8 with V = 2. The undeflected order J₀(φ)² vanishes at φ = 2.405 (τ ≈ 2.4). Measured here (target / mine):
The recoil energy is q²/2 ≈ 0.2, so for τ ≲ 2 the cloud hardly moves during the flash and the thin-grating formula holds.
try: Do nothing: the cloud is at rest, all of it in the k = 0 mine.
Switch the light on and leave it on, watching P_T: the orders fill, peak near t ≈ 2 after switching on, then the cloud starts to oscillate in the wells and the orders mix again.
Flash for about 2 time units, then observe: two clean side peaks in the momentum view, and the k = 0 peak nearly empty.
